pages.x: The khanate of Khiva, in an oasis on the Amu Darya river, raided Russian caravans and held Russians as slaves. In November 1839 the governor of Orenburg, Vasily Perovsky, set out to punish it with 5,000 men and 10,000 camels. A terrible winter killed most of the camels, and he had to turn back without ever seeing Khiva.

Russia learned to move slowly. It built lines of forts across the Kazakh steppe, put steamboats on the Aral Sea, and in 1853 stormed the fort of Ak-Mechet on the Syr Darya, held by the khanate of Kokand. Another line of forts pushed south from Siberia. Between the two lines lay Tashkent.

In 1865 the Russian commander Mikhail Chernyaev attacked Tashkent, the biggest city of Central Asia, with fewer than 2,000 men and without clear orders. His men climbed its long walls at night, and after two days of street fighting the city gave in. The tsar's government, which had wanted to wait, kept the prize.

General Konstantin von Kaufman, the first governor-general of Russian Turkestan, ruled from Tashkent almost like a king. In 1868 he marched against Bukhara and took Samarkand, Tamerlane's old capital, without a fight. While he chased the emir, a small garrison held the citadel of Samarkand against a rising for a week.

One of the defenders of Samarkand was a young painter, Vasily Vereshchagin. His pictures of the war showed its horror, not its glory. The most famous, The Apotheosis of War, painted in 1871, is a pyramid of skulls in the desert, dedicated, he wrote, to all great conquerors, past, present and to come.

In 1873 Kaufman sent columns across the deserts to Khiva from three sides. One had to turn back for lack of water, but the others met outside its walls, and the khan gave in. Khiva became a Russian protectorate, and its slave markets, where Persians and Russians had been sold for centuries, were closed.

Russia ended the khanate of Kokand in 1876 and made its rich Fergana valley a province. When the American Civil War had cut off cotton from the United States, Russia's mills had turned to Central Asia.
pages.fx: Cotton became the region's great crop. It fed Russian and later Soviet mills, and with its huge thirst for river water it helped, in the end, to dry up the Aral Sea.

pages.x: The Turkmen of the desert fought hardest. In 1879 they beat off an attack on their mud-walled fortress of Geok Tepe. General Skobelev came with a railway built across the sand, and in January 1881 blew a hole in the wall with a mine. Thousands of defenders and civilians were killed in the storm and the pursuit.

Merv gave in in 1884, and Russia's border reached Afghanistan, the buffer between it and British India. Central Asia was ruled as a colony until 1917, then by the Soviets, and the borders they drew became those of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan.
